item.title: What Is Infidelity? 3 Steps To Take If You Find Unfaithfulness In Your Life
item.description:
by Marcia Deah

Love is understood, in a historical way, as one of the great human vocations – but its counterspell has always been infidelity. This terrible, terrible betrayal that can tear apart not only another person, not only oneself, but whole families. – Junot Diaz

When I think of the question, what is infidelity? I think of a deep wound that travels through the body and pierces each part that creates the beautiful bonds of fidelity. To truly understand infidelity, you must truly experience fidelity.

So now the question is, what is fidelity? Fidelity is a commitment to steadfastness, loyalty, and faithfulness to the promises created in relationships, particularly romantic partners. It’s a deep level of intimacy that involves not only sex but also emotional faithfulness, relational loyalty, integrity in words and actions, and sexual exclusivity.

Emotional Faithfulness This involves being honest and transparent with your partner. It protects the emotional bonds the partners have created through consistency, communication, and trust. It requires dedication to not form secret or intimate attachments outside the relationship.

Relational Loyalty It involves keeping the promises between you and your partner, showing up consistently and always prioritizing your relationship over temptations and possible distractions.

Integrity in Your Words and Actions This includes always telling the truth, having open and honest communication, no matter how hard it is to say or to hear. You must align your behaviors with your values. You must be trustworthy even when your partner is not around.

Sexual Exclusivity This is exactly how it sounds. Not breaking the physical boundaries you have agreed upon. In monogamous relationships specifically, it is the choice not to engage in sexual or romantic relations with others.

In simplest terms, fidelity is exactly what the scripture tells us. Fidelity is Love. Love is patient and kind; love does not envy or boast; it is not arrogant or rude. It does not insist on its own way; it is not irritable or resentful; it does not rejoice at wrongdoing, but rejoices with the truth. Love bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. – 1 Corinthians 13: 4-7

When fidelity is broken, we enter the realms of infidelity. Once we are in these waters, it can be like trying to swim in the ocean against the current. If you continue to go against the current, the harder it will be to stay afloat. However, if you start to go with the current, eventually, with intention, with faith, with love, and with the following three steps, you can overcome the depths of infidelity.

Three Steps for the Partner Who Was Unfaithful

Take full ownership without defensiveness

It is natural to be defensive, even when we are in the wrong. Infidelity can only be a factor in a committed and love-filled relationship. If you are reading this article, I guess that betraying your partner was not a proud moment for you. This is why it is important to acknowledge the choices you made and the impact they had on everyone involved.

This means taking full ownership of your behaviors. You cannot minimize your actions. You must eliminate the urge to defend yourself. Avoid statements such as “yes, but…” Taking ownership will require humility and be foundational in the repair of your relationship.

Explore the internal drivers behind the affair

This may be one of the hardest parts of the repair process. Telling your partner, whom you hurt and betrayed, that you felt a void in your relationship. At times, this has absolutely nothing to do with your partner; it may be internal factors. Unfortunately, it is often more than one reason.

Could it be an emotional disconnection? Do you feel that you and your partner are emotionally aligned? Are you avoiding the truth? Are there needs that you have that are being unmet, or vice versa, are there needs that you are not willing to meet? Are there some personal wounds that have not been addressed or not healed? Understanding the “why” is important because then we can fix the issues instead of repeating the same patterns that caused the disruptions.

It is important to understand yourself and what you need to invoke true change and partnership. These are some questions to begin with, but you will need to explore them not only with your partner, but with the assistance of a licensed couples therapist (such as me). A licensed therapist would be beneficial simply for support and guidance, and most importantly, an unbiased perspective.

Offer consistency, transparency, and repair behaviors

Again, this could be achieved with you and your partner; however, counsel from a licensed provider will reap better results. There will be questions that your partner has. You will need to answer them with care and honesty.

Your partner will need a lot of reassurance and gentleness. Showing them that you are reliable will be crucial because you have shown yourself unreliable with their heart. Being empathetic will go a long way toward re-earning your partner’s trust and regaining clarity.

3 Steps for the Partner Who Discovered the Affair

Stabilize your internal world

You have just been hit with a big fat boot to the chest. The air in your lungs has been snatched from your body suddenly, and now you are expected to breathe anyway. It feels unfair, and it is! You made a commitment to your partner, and they broke your agreement. So, before you can begin to understand what caused the rupture, you must first slow down your nervous system and stabilize your emotions.

Utilize grounding techniques and learn how to breathe steadily again. Utilize healthy coping skills that will assist you in working through the infidelity. Try journaling your journey so that you can recognize where you are healing and where you need more work. Talk it out with someone you trust but be careful with this option as it can have repercussions. Your goal needs to be clarity, so you have to work on reducing reactivity as much as possible.

Identify what you need to feel safe

Remember safety is always the top priority and the backbone of the operation. Without felt safety, you will not be able to work through anything. Your emotional safety will require honesty, transparency, and reassurance from your partner. Identifying your physical safety will mean holding on to your space, your boundaries, and even your routines.

A big part will also be relational safety. You will want to know the whys and, at times, certain details. Understand that some details are unnecessary to know. Knowing certain details can be more detrimental than just leaving it be. When you can identify your needs, this will help calm some of the chaos.

Express your experience without self-blame

With your partner, share the impact their behaviors have on you and your relationship. Avoid further accusations while remaining true to how the actual betrayal has affected you. When you can talk through these hurts with your partner, it helps you reclaim your voice and helps the relationship move forward positively toward repairing.

Three Steps for Healing as a Couple

Rebuild safety together

As stated above, the relationship will need the restoration of emotional stability. This will look like creating predictable routines and communication with one another. Sometimes this may entail overly communicating with your partner until trust is restored. You will need to practice being transparent with one another, so you do not feel the need to babysit your partner’s every move. It is not fair to you, them, or the relationship.

It does not create a sense of stability; it creates surveillance. You need to agree on boundaries that will help you both feel grounded and supported. Remember that even though betrayal is the reason you are in this situation, there were still underlying factors that contributed to this.

So, slow down, allow the conflict to settle through your hard work, and do not overwhelm yourselves. Think of safety as your soil. Without your safety, nothing will grow. Read my article on forgiveness because this will also play a major factor in your safety.

Rebuild understanding through honest dialogue

Since you have safety as your soil, and forgiveness as your fertilizer, you have already begun the growth process. Since you are doing the work to grow, you can now make meaning of what has happened. In this step, you will practice sharing your emotions without attacking each other (easier said than done).

The best way to do this is to listen with an ear for understanding, not to defend yourself or your behavior. As hard as it will be, you must seek to understand not only the impact, but also the unmet needs on both ends. In therapy, we can work on your relationship narrative. What was the relationship before, what is it now, what do you see it as in the future?

Understanding your story will help reduce confusion, resentment, and assumptions in your relationship. You will begin to see the full picture rather being stuck in your own hurt, story, guilt, shame, or unforgiveness.

Rebuild connection through intentional repair

In this step, you will create a new relationship – the final draft. This will not be your story moving forward. It will be a chapter of your past. You will need to practice consistency with your partner. Be determined to repair using some of the skills I mentioned above, such as empathy, reassurance, accountability, honesty, openness, forgiveness, etc.

It will also be helpful to rebuild your trust through small, steady, and reliable action steps. Relationships thrive from intimacy. Yes, you will have to be intimate with your partner again. You have to be willing to be vulnerable for real change to take place in your lives. You will have to intentionally re-establish emotional intimacy and even physical intimacy.

You will need to create goals and shared meaning. What is your vision for the relationship, and how can you create rituals or routines to ensure your healthy relationship? Your healing is not about the old relationship; it’s about building a new, stronger, safer, and more connected relationship than ever before.

These last three steps happen simultaneously with the previous steps. You can heal; your relationship is not only survivable, but it is capable of pure, undeniable happiness and love. I would love to be the therapist you choose to help you through this fragile time in your relationship. Book a session with me and let’s work toward rebuilding your connection together.

item.title: Is it Justified Guilt or Shame?
item.description:
Guilt and shame have been a part of the human experience from the dawn of man. After both Eve and Adam ate the fruit in the Garden of Eden, one of the first emotions they felt was described as what we know today as shame. “Then the eyes of both of them were opened, and they realized they were naked; so they sewed fig leaves together and made coverings for themselves.” (Genesis 3:7, NIV) Because sin entered the world, they became self-aware and felt ashamed.

Guilt in the Bible is connected to specific actions or sins. It’s the awareness that you have done something wrong, which leads to repentance and corrective action. An example of this can be found in Psalm 51 when David expresses guilt for his specific wrongdoings and seeks restoration.

Guilt is meant to signal to us that we may have done something wrong, disappointed God, or let someone else down. In small doses, guilt can be helpful because it encourages us to pause to analyze our behavior, take accountability, and correct our behavior.

Shame, however, works differently. While guilt focuses on behavior, shame targets identity. Guilt tells you that you did something wrong, while shame tells you that something is wrong with you. This is an important distinction because guilt can lead to growth, but shame leads to hiding and self-condemnation.

For some people, guilt is more than a fleeting feeling or a minor emotional response. Instead, it can become a default emotional state or a lens through which they view themselves and the world, and can lead to chronic shame.

This pattern can be both exhausting and deeply frustrating. Why do some people default to guilt? Is it linked to Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)? Does it relate to other negative emotions? Or is it rooted in learned patterns from early life experiences?

Let’s explore the complex interplay of ADHD, emotional regulation, cognitive biases, and environmental factors that can lead someone to habitually default to guilt. Most importantly, let’s learn how to break the cycle.

Understanding Guilt

Before diving deep into why someone might default to guilt, it’s important to define the emotion itself. Guilt is an internal signal that arises when a person believes they have violated a moral, social, or personal standard or have violated God’s law. It focuses on behavior.

It tells you that “I did something wrong.” Shame, however, focuses on self or “I am a bad person.” While guilt can motivate actions, chronic guilt can create anxiety, depression, and a sense of inadequacy.

Defaulting to guilt means that you tend to immediately assume responsibility for negative outcomes, even when the situation is minor, ambiguous, or not entirely in your control. Your brain has a preset mode of sorts. Any mistake, conflict, or unmet expectation triggers guilt automatically.

ADHD and the Guilt Loop

For many people with ADHD, guilt becomes an almost automatic reaction. ADHD affects executive functioning, which includes planning, prioritizing, remembering tasks, and managing time. When these systems don’t work smoothly, it’s easy to forget responsibility, miss deadlines, and overlook details.

Some people with ADHD may feel an overwhelming guilt in response to their failures, even if they didn’t intend to fail. This happens because people with ADHD have brains that amplify errors and then ruminate on them.

Emotional regulation, another area often impacted by ADHD, makes it difficult to step back from feelings of guilt. A minor oversight can quickly spiral into a cycle of self-condemnation. This is where guilt feeds anxiety, shame, and even physical tension.

Other negative emotions can feel like guilt

Anyone, even those without ADHD, can have guilt as a default emotion out of a pattern or habit. Any negative emotion that they feel, from embarrassment to unmet expectations, can manifest itself as guilt. That’s because guilt rarely exists in isolation but often intertwines with shame, anxiety, and low self-esteem.

When guilt escalates, it can morph into shame. It can feel crushing and can affect your self-image. If you’re already experiencing low self-esteem, guilt will be amplified. Soon, you believe that every misstep is a confirmation of your personal inadequacies.

Anxiety can also contribute to default guilt. When anxiety is present, the mind constantly scans for what might go wrong or what could have been done better. Instead of evaluating a situation realistically, the anxious brain jumps straight to self-blame. You might find yourself apologizing excessively, replaying conversations, or assuming responsibility for other people’s emotions.

Learned Guilt and Responsibility

Default guilt is often learned early in childhood as a way to survive emotionally, relationally, or even spiritually. When a child grows up in an environment where mistakes are exaggerated or their emotional needs are dismissed, they often start to feel a deep sense of guilt.

If a child’s behavior dictates whether or not there’s harmony in the house, they will see each bad behavior as a catastrophic mistake, and guilt then becomes a protective strategy. This guilt becomes their automatic response to every mistake made, even when guilt isn’t warranted.

Children with ADHD are particularly vulnerable to this pattern. Because their behavior is often corrected more frequently, misunderstood, or labeled as careless or disruptive, they may internalize the belief that they’re always the problem. This repeated feedback trains their brain to assume fault automatically. Guilt becomes much less about what actually happened and more about their attempts to prevent future disapproval.

In Christian homes, this pattern can become even more prevalent because it’s often unintentionally reinforced. When obedience is emphasized without equal attention to grace, a sensitive or neurodivergent child may confuse spiritual growth with emotional self-punishment.

In these situations, a child learns to monitor themselves constantly, searching for what they did wrong rather than resting and relying on God’s grace. Conviction then leads to self-shame instead of repentance and restoration.

Therapeutic Help

It’s important to be able to distinguish between justified guilt and shame. For people who live with ADHD or long-standing emotional patterns, default guilt can become a part of their life and can undermine their self-esteem and even their spiritual health.

If guilt has become a learned or neurological response that has developed to cope or avoid conflict, you may benefit from working with a licensed therapist. A trained professional understands emotional patterns and neurological differences from a biblical perspective.

ADHD informed therapists recognize that chronic guilt is how the brain might process mistakes, expectations, and emotional feedback. A therapist will help you work through this automatic guilt response and provide you with practical tools for emotional regulation. They will teach you how to do more realistic self-assessments, which are often more difficult for people with ADHD.

Therapy can help you figure out where justified guilt is serving its intended purpose of growth, and where it becomes misplaced or excessive. You will learn to recognize your automatic guilt responses. You’ll also learn how to challenge these ideas so you respond to mistakes, emotions, and relational interactions with appropriate and healthy responses. Through this process, you will be able to use guilt as the tool it’s intended to be rather than a constant condemnation.

A Christian therapist will also use a biblical base to remind you that God’s correction is rooted in His love for us. It is not to keep you in a state of depression or anxiety. Guilt is meant to convict, not cause internalized shame.

God’s correction is specific, loving, and restorative. Shame is vague, consistent, and condemning. In therapy, you will learn to quiet the constant voice of misplaced guilt and shame so that the loving voice of God can speak truth into your life.

Living in Freedom

Healing from default guilt will give you a tremendous sense of freedom. You shouldn’t lower your standards or avoid responsibility to achieve that goal, but rather use guilt to form your spiritual and moral boundaries. When you break free of the guilt loop, you will begin to relate to yourself with the same grace that God extends to you.

You can start this process with a Christian therapist on this site. Reach out to the reception office to connect with someone who can help you find freedom from shame.

item.title: Cultivating Female Friendships in a Small Group
item.description:
Ministry in the modern world might look quite different from what it did in Jesus’ day. We don’t ride donkeys on the way to synagogue or have Jesus with us in the flesh. Even though the world looks different, we can still use biblical principles and Jesus’ example to guide us in ministering to others effectively.

If you’re in a women’s ministry or are a small group or Bible study leader, you’re likely longing to see more than just polite conversation and surface-level connection in your group.

Jesus aimed for that too. He ministered to crowds, but He invested deeply in a small group of disciples. Within that circle, genuine friendship, accountability, and love took root. As a leader, you’re invited to follow His example and create a place where women can experience the same type of safe and authentic connections.

Love and Inclusiveness

And let us consider how we may spur one another on toward love and good deeds… – Hebrews 10:24, NIV

Christian friendship is ultimately the continual act of helping each other grow closer to Jesus. The foundation of Christianity is love, as seen in Jesus’ ultimate sacrifice. And when you approach your ministry with the same spirit of love, you will see fruit. When you model the action of love as a leader, you will begin to see that same spirit manifest in the members of your group because love is contagious.

Praying together regularly with intention is a great way to model love. Prayer not only invites the presence of God into your relationships but also encourages transparency and empathy among participants.

Not everyone will be at the same place in their spiritual life, so be sensitive to those who might not feel comfortable praying aloud. The same goes for Scripture reading. Many people, even good readers, struggle with reading in front of others. Feel free to ask for volunteers, but as a leader, be prepared to read the Scriptures yourself.

Practicing patience is another way to ensure that your group is full of love and acceptance. While you might not get an ideal blend of personalities in your group, keep in mind that the purpose is to learn how to love people who are vastly different from us. This is the same love Jesus offered and still does today.

Build trust

Therefore encourage one another and build each other up… – 1 Thessalonians 5:11, NIV

If you want to help the women in your small group develop meaningful and long-lasting friendships, establish trust in the group. Trust is what helps relationships grow.

One important way to build trust is to guard your tongue and encourage other members to do the same. Scripture says, “Those who guard their lips preserve their lives, but those who speak rashly will come to ruin.” (Proverbs 13:3, NIV) In abiding by this, you can foster a place where women feel comfortable and secure.

The group should be a safe space where women can talk about their feelings, ask questions they might be too afraid to ask elsewhere, and share the innermost parts of their lives. If gossip or harsh judgment takes root, your small group is no longer considered a safe harbor for those involved. Even worse, it could hurt people or harm the larger church body.

Encourage your members to keep each other’s private lives private. Lovingly stop conversations if they turn toward gossip. Create a lesson, preferably early in the group meetings, that discusses the potential harm that can come when tongues go unguarded. When a woman knows her heart is safe in your hands and in the hands of the other members of your small group, she will begin to open up. That trust is where true sisterhood begins to grow.

Encourage authenticity

Therefore confess your sins to each other and pray for each other that you may be healed. – James 5:16, NIV

If you want to move past surface-level pleasantries and build trust, you need to take off your mask. As a leader, the speed of the group’s intimate growth is often determined by your own level of transparency. When you are willing to share your own struggles, mistakes, and sins, you give the other women permission to do the same. Authenticity creates a ripple effect by breaking down walls of perfection that so often keep people isolated.

Encourage a culture where it’s okay not to have it all together. Remind your group that the goal isn’t to have all the answers or to present a perfect, polished life, but to show up to your gatherings exactly as you are. When you create an environment where vulnerability is met with grace rather than a lecture, you will mirror the heart of Jesus, who welcomed the weary and burdened with open arms.

Carry one another’s burdens

Carry each other’s burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ. – Galatians 6:2, NIV

Authentic friendship often moves beyond the living room or the church basement. While the deep conversations you have during your Bible study are the catalyst for connection, the glue that holds the group together is how you show up for each other during life’s big and even mundane moments.

Encourage members of your group to look for practical ways to serve one another outside of your scheduled meeting time. Organize a meal train for a sister who is sick, offer to watch someone’s children so she can have a moment of rest, or simply send a text of encouragement in the middle of a stressful work week.

When women see that they’re cared for in real, practical ways, their hearts will soften, and they will be more willing to engage in the deeper, spiritual aspects of the ministry.

Work toward healing

He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds. – Psalm 147:3, NIV

As you strive toward depth in your small group ministry, remember that some of these women carry wounds that go deeper than a weekly study or coffee date can reach. You need to exercise patience as your members work through trauma and open up about the most guarded parts of their lives.

Seek the Holy Spirit for guidance as you plan your small group sessions. Be open to the movement of the Spirit as you allow Him to guide conversations and relationships. Ask the women in the group what topics they want to discuss and study, and be open to suggestions. You never know what hidden burdens people carry. A small group is a prime opportunity for them to explore these topics that need the most.

While you can pray and love on each other in a small group, as the leader, you may not be equipped to handle all the trauma in their lives. Part of loving your sisters well is recognizing when a burden requires a specialized level of care.

Just as you would encourage a friend with a physical ailment to see a doctor, you should be open to lovingly suggesting Christian therapy for mental and emotional health. Integrating the idea of professional counseling into your conversations helps to remove the taboo and acknowledges that God often uses the wisdom of trained therapists to help untangle all the complex parts of our mental and emotional lives.

Doing life together

Cultivating deep, Christ-centered friendship in a small group setting is a process. It requires courage to be honest, the discipline to keep confidences, and the wisdom to point each other toward both God and the practical resources He provides for healing.

As you lead, remember that you’re following in the footsteps of the greatest teacher. With His help, your small group can truly become a place where authentic friendships grow and can become a safe harbor for every woman who walks through the door.

To learn more about caring for a small group or the resources available, reach out to a Christian counselor.

item.title: Getting to the Root of Anger Problems
item.description:
If you have ever lost your temper to the point of getting physical, raising your voice, or saying things that you later regret, you are in the majority. Everyone gets angry on occasion, and often an angry response is warranted, logical, or at least understandable. However, if your default response is anger, there might be something else going on.

If it doesn’t take much for you to fly off the handle and say or do things you regret, anger could be a problem area. If you look back on your behavior with embarrassment and shame, you might have anger problems. This might be a sensitive topic for you, but it can be resolved in time.

The Anger Iceberg

While anger is often destructive and harmful, sometimes it can be helpful. As Jesus once told His disciples, “‘…For the mouth speaks what the heart is full of.’” (Luke 6:45, NIV) In other words, the way we act, the things we say, and our emotional responses show what is going on inside of us in the deep, hidden parts of us.

We show how we are feeling with words or actions, even when it is unintentional. Sometimes our emotions are so close to the surface that others see them long before we say or do anything.

Anger is an incredibly complex emotion, and it’s not always easy to see what it is connected to. For example, it’s understandable to get annoyed when someone cuts you off in traffic. It’s a selfish thing to do, it’s potentially dangerous, and it blocks your progress. You might curse quietly or demonstrate your frustration to the other driver with gestures and facial expressions.

However, if you have anger problems, something as simple and common as being cut off in traffic might spark an inferno of rage that effectively ruins your entire day. If your angry reactions to triggering events are disproportionate or hard to control, there is likely something more going on beneath the surface.

When Anger Becomes a Problem

Few people like getting angry, even when it seems to be their default emotion. This is because anger is a physical emotion. It takes physical effort to express, whether it is in gestures, words, or emotions. Anger uses up physical resources whether you express it or not, and any positive change rarely comes from it. The more intense the anger, the more negative consequences come from the outbursts.

To be clear, anger is not always a problem. Sometimes it is a useful motivator that helps us clear obstructions in our path or gain clarity over murky issues. However, it is a problem if it leads to physical altercations, yelling or screaming, if it leads your loved ones to feel unsafe around you, or if it is your singular response to every issue. When any behavior is a default or an extreme, it is usually masking an unresolved issue.

The Root of Anger Problems

As in the case of being angry with bad drivers, people most often experience anger in response to logical things. You do not have anger problems if you periodically become angry over understandable things. Anger becomes a problem when it is ongoing, disproportionate, or disconnected from immediate events, and if it continuously affects your relationships, whether personal or professional.

You might be avoiding dealing with your anger problems because you are aware that they are attached to other issues that you are unwilling to face. Ignoring issues does not make them go away; it’s best to face what is potentially going on.

Your health and daily routine contribute more to your overall mental health than you might realize.

The most obvious things that contribute to anger issues are stress, sleep deprivation, poor diet, physical illness, and emotional turmoil.

You might be facing all these things at once, in which case, there is little wonder why you have anger problems. When you ignore these seemingly minor issues over time, they develop into an unhealthy lifestyle. This kind of lifestyle compromises all the relationships in your life.

Blocked Goals You could ask yourself whether you have anger issues or whether you are permanently frustrated. The two are not the same, though they are frequently connected. Sometimes people develop anger problems because of how they deal with their frustrations.

For example, you might be stressed out as you work on an important assignment when the internet stops working. This is obviously frustrating because it has blocked an urgent goal, and you feel helpless and out of control, on top of being stressed. You might deal with this frustration by crashing out and raging; objects will be broken, and curse words will be heard.

When you are frequently frustrated to the point of rage, you need to adjust the way you cope with things. You might need to practically address the situation, such as changing your internet service provider, or you might need to build a new skill set, such as time management, organization, or communication skills.

Channeling your focus and energy into developing new skills will give a more useful avenue for the energy that would otherwise be devoted to tantrums and triggers. This also gives you a feeling of control as you focus on something that you can manage.

Perceived Injustice and Disrespect

You could experience anger problems because of how you feel others are treating you. Anger most commonly is a response to things like injustice, perceived disrespect, and feeling devalued by others. Although you might not want to hear it, your angry responses to the things currently happening to you might be linked to painful experiences in your past.

If you constantly felt overlooked in childhood, if your preferences were never considered, or if you were constantly criticized over issues that were not your fault, these situations will likely be triggers for you until you begin addressing them.

A Cover for Pain

Though it might be uncomfortable to hear, anger is most commonly a mask for pain. Men especially have a hard time being vulnerable and honest with their emotions, and it feels safer to express anger than it is to show that you are hurt, afraid, insecure, or sad. It’s deeply unpleasant to feel helpless, especially when others look to you for leadership and strength. Anger and rage feel like empowering emotions, even though they cause more harm than good.

There is no easy or quick way to resolve anger problems because most often they are connected to deeper, more personal issues. Don’t let that discourage you from facing your issues head-on. The past is never truly in the past, and our wounds only begin to heal when we acknowledge them.

Sometimes, however, a breakthrough comes in ways you would have never expected. You might benefit from adjusting your routine, changing your approach to frustrating blockages, or having some honest conversations with a counselor or close friend.

Anger is not always a problem, but it is also not an empowering or sustainable response. You are not doomed to stay trapped with anger problems, but you must be willing to be vulnerable and honest with someone.

Just as new life appears after a forest fire has ravaged nature, so can there be fruit in the life that has been burned by rage. The sooner you begin addressing your anger problems, the sooner you can develop healthier responses to life’s frustrating developments.

If you would rather speak with someone to arrange counseling sessions, our reception team will help connect you with someone.

item.title: How Perfectionism Can Contribute to Work Burnout
item.description:
If you are someone who needs a high level of control, for everything to go your way, and for high standards in every task, you probably already know you are a perfectionist. Many workplaces encourage, champion, and even require certain levels of perfectionism to get the job done.

Perfectionism is a key factor in meeting deadlines, making progress, and maintaining high standards of output. However, perfectionism is also the main contributor to low morale in the workplace and eventual work burnout. It is essential to observe and confront the effects of perfectionism, both for the longevity and the health of any project.

The Roots of Perfectionism

Some people have realized that it pays to be orderly, tidy, focused, and punctual. These types of people believe the success of work projects often rests on these things. These are not only habits, they are also attitudes, and they are unquestionably beneficial.

On the other hand, some people cannot focus unless everything in their environment meets the standards they have set, and their progress and mood can often be severely affected if things do not go their way. People in the latter category are far less happy in their careers and far more likely to experience work burnout.

There is a vast difference between preferring and striving for optimum results, and not being able to function unless every aspect of the project is perfect. There are neat people, and then there are perfectionists. One is a personality trait, and the other is a trauma response.

Perfectionism is a bigger issue than most people are willing to admit, though they know something isn’t right in themselves. Their career might be soaring as their relationships crumble, but they simply crack down and focus even harder on their work.

Often, it is only when progress at work begins stalling that they can finally admit to themselves that they are burnt out and need help. By this time, the damage is often already done. If it’s not their personal lives that have suffered, it’s their physical health. In many cases, it is both. Perfectionism isn’t a tool that helps achievement; it is a coping mechanism that usually results in isolation, exhaustion, and depression.

At their core, most perfectionists feel out of control in their personal lives, even though it may seem that they have everything together. They control their worlds through micromanaging and overachieving, but that only contributes to the damage.

If they don’t end up experiencing work burnout, then their colleagues, teams, and employees soon will. Perfectionism is not about success, achievements, standards, or goals. It is about trying to fix something internal, regarding all of the things you believe have more value than you do. When your self-worth is linked to your achievements, failure and perceived failure are your biggest threats. Perfectionism is an avoidant behavior, though you don’t know anything different. There is still time to confront yourself and make a change, and the sooner you start, the sooner you heal.

How Perfectionism Contributes to Work Burnout

It makes you a harsh critic When you are a perfectionist, you are your own harshest critic, but you are also a critic by nature. You find flaws where others don’t. This can damage relationships with colleagues, as they may feel held to unrealistic expectations.

It makes you procrastinate Rather than propel projects, perfectionism often causes you to delay them. You are held back from progress because you are afraid of failure. It is exhausting to always be caught in the tension of needing to make progress, but holding back because of fear. Procrastinating in this way is like endlessly treading water: you get tired from going nowhere.

It has you always planning but never acting Related to fear of failure and procrastination, perfectionism can get you caught in the planning phase for far too long, inhibiting progress. If you are the leader of a team, this attitude can likely filter down to the workers. Knowing your strict need for perfection, they’ll likely overplan rather than risk disappointing you with weak results.

It makes you obsessed Perfectionists are not simply detail-oriented. They pour all of their focus and energy into the details of a project. Not only is this exhausting and frustrating, but it also causes you to lose sight of the bigger picture. When you forget about the why of a job, work burnout will swiftly follow. Don’t let your projects perish because you lose sight of the bigger picture.

It makes you overly sensitive to criticism Every aspect of a workplace benefits from evaluation and feedback occasionally. This is how you know you’re making progress and that it is in the right direction.

However, perfectionists find it hard not to take feedback personally. When your self-worth is entirely dependent on success, even helpful advice feels like criticism. To avoid work burnout, it is helpful to learn to take advice, feedback, and criticism when necessary.

It causes you to dwell on failures Perfectionism will have you fixating on failures, both your own and those around you. You begin to focus on everything that went wrong, and rarely ever celebrate what went right.

Nothing kills morale faster than successes and breakthroughs that go unnoticed. What is the point of doing anything if your achievements are never acknowledged? On the other hand, hearing praise for a job well done is fuel for even the weariest of workers, yourself included.

It is never satisfying Perfectionism always leads to work burnout because it never feels like you’ve achieved enough. It is an endless journey through the wilderness of ignored achievements toward the Promised Land, but it never concludes.

One by one, your team burns out until you’re alone in chasing the mirages of success and contentment. Until you begin reflecting on what is driving your perfectionism, you may have a bleak future to look forward to, one devoid of satisfaction and contentment.

Make New Choices

The good news is that we can learn new things. We can change, grow, improve, heal, and right our wrongs. It all starts with self-reflection and a willingness to embrace change.

You’ve done the best you can until now. Even in your failures, your efforts were impressive. Even if you never met another goal, you would still have worth because of who you are. You might have had to work hard to gain respect, affection, and acceptance, but none of those things fully define you. You are more than the sum of your failures and successes. In fact, below is the truth about who God says you are:

You are God’s child “See what great love the Father has lavished on us, that we should be called children of God!” (1 John 3:1).

You are loved unconditionally “I am convinced that nothing can ever separate us from God’s love” (Romans 8:38-39).

You are God’s masterpiece (handiwork) “For we are God’s handiwork, created in Christ Jesus to do good works” (Ephesians 2:10).

You are fearfully and wonderfully made “I praise you because I am fearfully and wonderfully made” (Psalm 139:14).

Perfectionism will always keep you busy if you allow it. You will forget what it feels like to rest, recharge, and reflect on your journey. You will always feel as if you haven’t done enough and don’t deserve a break.

The first step in confronting perfectionism is to interrupt it by simply stopping. This could look like taking the day off from work or booking some extended time off. It requires you to lean into whatever you have been avoiding. If it helps, remind yourself that sometimes the smallest changes bring about the best results. You’ve got what it takes to make the necessary changes to your life.

It’s a lot easier to make big life changes when you have someone helping you. If you would like to meet with a counselor, please consult our online directory. Alternatively, you may speak with our reception team, who would be delighted to help you find the right counselor to meet with.

item.title: Progressive Parenting and Behavioral Problems in Children
item.description:
Across America, a shift is underway that most parents do not anticipate. They’re working hard to keep their children happy and genuinely believe that they are doing their best. Still, behavioral problems, including defiance at home, struggles in school, and difficulty respecting authority, surface. The parents find themselves confused and exhausted, wondering how their best intentions led to these challenging outcomes.

We often find the answer in the parenting philosophy that has shaped American culture for over 50 years. Progressive parenting has emphasized freedom and emotional expression while minimizing structure and boundaries. The result is an environment where children lack the framework they need to develop self-control and emotional regulation.

The absence of this intentional training leads to children facing a world without the internal compass needed to make wise choices. Many families face a challenge centered on a message that has defined good parenting as prioritizing a child’s emotional expression at the expense of necessary boundaries. Biblical wisdom serves us well in these situations:

Start children off on the way they should go, and even when they are old they will not turn from it. – Proverbs 22:6, NIV

The Progressive Parenting Movement and Its Promises

The psychological mainstream started in the 1960s and made a dramatic claim that reshaped parenting for generations. This claim from mental health professionals emphasizes that parents who don’t allow children to express their feelings freely create an avenue for mental health problems for their children. Society began to define it as understanding and appropriately responding to all emotional expressions.

This suggested a promise that children raised with maximum freedom and minimal boundaries would grow into confident, emotionally healthy adults with strong self-esteem. This approach led parents to believe that structure and discipline could damage their children’s psyches, and that unlimited emotional support and autonomy would allow them to flourish naturally.

Advocates for progressive parenting have reshaped biblical warnings regarding harsh parenting into something that was never meant to be. There was no distinction between the kind of harsh control that crushes a child and the loving limits that create security.

Parents were left in a confusing position, trying to navigate between what felt like only two options. Some had grown up under overly strict parents, and this philosophy felt like permission to do things differently.

Why Parents Embraced the Progressive Philosophy

There are several reasons why the progressive parenting message resonated so profoundly with parents during this time. Many had grown up in households run by strict rules, harsh punishment, and little emotional warmth. These parents remembered feeling unheard, controlled, and afraid of making mistakes.

When mental health professionals began discussing how traditional parenting approaches had been damaging, these parents listened eagerly and hoped for better outcomes. The philosophy they heard aligned with a broader cultural shift toward individual autonomy, self-expression, and the rethinking of traditional authority structures.

Parents wanted a close relationship with their children, and they saw the promise of this in progressive parenting. Progressive parenting sought to eliminate this discomfort rather than being an authoritative figure in their child’s life. Parents were encouraged to see themselves as a resource. This meant using reason rather than consequences to allow children to regulate their own behavior.

In times of conflict, parents were taught to process feelings rather than establish clear expectations and follow through with consistent discipline. Even though this seemed compassionate in the moment, it failed to equip children with the internal structure they needed to manage themselves effectively.

Fifty Years Later and the Rise in Behavioral Problems

After five decades of progressive parenting, we are seeing a significant decline in children’s mental health. Christian counselors are seeing an increase in behavioral problems rather than the decrease that was promised when parents first began implementing this approach to raising children.

Some of the problems include struggles with impulsivity, difficulty delaying gratification, and failure to consider consequences before acting. This also resulted in less respect for authority figures and a tendency to view rules as optional suggestions rather than necessary guidelines.

Conservative parents who tend to use authoritative parenting with warmth and boundaries have raised children who have better mental health. Those who have adopted the more permissive approach that progressive parenting promotes tend to see more mental health issues among children. This supports the Scriptures about parenting.

Discipline your children, and they will give you peace; they will bring you the delights you desire. – Proverbs 29:17, NIV

There is a peace that can emerge from the security children feel within proper boundaries. However, progressive parenting has taught parents that this structure is to be feared. Christian counselors often encounter families suffering the consequences of this cultural message. Parents come in exhausted and confused because the expert advice has led to an increasingly anxious, defiant child.

These parents seek help because they love their child deeply and realize they have been misled about what love requires. They are beginning to understand that the approach they chose in hopes of demonstrating care ended up undermining their child’s development and mental health.

How Behavioral Problems Develop in Progressive Households

A child raised without clear boundaries often exhibits specific patterns that will emerge over time and create lasting challenges. They have never learned to pause and consider consequences, so they become impulsive. These children struggle to understand empathy for others because they have been accustomed to their own needs and desires being put first.

Progressively raised children who face disappointment or frustration may experience an emotional meltdown because they do not know the resilience that comes from working through complicated feelings. These children often struggle in structured environments, such as school, simply because they have not been raised to follow rules they didn’t create or accept consequences they don’t understand.

From a biblical perspective, parenting includes love and limits, affection and authority. God demonstrated his perfect love while maintaining clear expectations for his children. This discipline was not out of anger or harshness, but from a desire to shape character and guide them toward wisdom. This type of parenting directly opposes progressive parenting philosophy.

Children who grow up without this framework are often overwhelmed by a world that doesn’t adjust to their desires. They may experience anxiety due to the lack of internal structure to help them manage external demands. Relationships become difficult because they have not been taught to consider others’ needs alongside their own.

What Children Actually Need Beyond Cultural Trends

It’s been demonstrated that children thrive best under what is called authoritative parenting. This style combines high warmth with high expectations and looks remarkably similar to biblical parenting principles.

A parent who uses a balanced approach maintains clear rules and consistent consequences, while showing genuine affection and responding to the child’s emotional needs. When they make a decision, they explain their reasoning, listen to their child’s perspective, and make adjustments when needed, while maintaining their role as an authority figure.

A clear hierarchy and set of expectations established in Scripture counters the progressive parenting philosophy. Christian counselors emphasize to parents that this biblical model doesn’t mean they must be harsh or emotionally distant. They encourage parents to embrace the balance that God designed: a love expressed through affection and accountability, warmth paired with wisdom, and nurture combined with structure.

Moving Forward and Reclaiming Healthy Boundaries

Many parents who realize they have been influenced by progressive parenting may feel discouraged and wonder if it’s too late to make changes. Children are resilient and responsive to positive shifts. Parents are encouraged to take the first step and understand that setting boundaries doesn’t make parenting harsh.

Christian counselors can support parents in this transition and help the family establish a new pattern that reflects biblical principles rather than cultural trends. If you would like more information, reach out to the local Christian Counseling service in your area.

item.title: When Every Day Feels Like Trauma
item.description:
When you think about trauma, it’s usually framed as an isolated event. Something that has happened to you that has caused a great deal of havoc on your emotions and on other parts of your life. But for some people, trauma isn’t isolated to a singular event or something easily pinpointed. Some people feel like they’re going through trauma every day, which can make ordinary experiences feel dangerous and overwhelming.

Understanding Chronic Trauma

Chronic trauma is something experts call complex trauma or C-PTSD, and it’s more common than you might think. It stems from prolonged, repeated, or inescapable traumatic events. It’s seen in cases of ongoing abuse or neglect, particularly in childhood. The intense feelings you get when you are going through trauma stretch beyond a singular event to affect core emotional regulation, relationships, sense of self, and even bodily functions.

Here’s the part that often surprises people, at least those who aren’t experiencing it. Not everyone who feels constantly on edge has experienced abuse, neglect, or any clearly identifiable traumatic event. Sometimes trauma-like feelings don’t come from a singular trauma at all. It comes simply from living in a world that can be unnervingly unpredictable, relentlessly demanding, and downright exhausting.

Causes of Chronic Trauma That Aren’t Related to a Single Trauma

There are several ways that you can develop chronic trauma symptoms that aren’t directly related to a singular traumatic event.

Your childhood environment contributes to how you process the world around you as an adult. If you grow up in a household that demands perfection, has high expectations, or doles out subtle criticism, your nervous system learns to stay alert.

Through experience, you have learned to always anticipate what’s next or what could go wrong as a protective shield against negative consequences. This learned nervous system response will continue into adulthood and will manifest as perfectionism or overwork.

Chronic stress in adulthood can have a similar effect on your nervous system. Long-term financial struggles, high-pressure jobs, caregiving responsibilities, or even living in a community where safety is uncertain can all contribute. These stressors train your body to stay in a state of high alert. While these stressors aren’t as definable as a catastrophic ordeal, they can make daily life feel like a test of endurance. Triggers that seem harmless to most can send you reeling.

Even experiences that feel normal on the surface, such as balancing school, work, and family, can contribute to this state. When life demands more than the energy you have, your nervous system can mistake these chronic pressures for real threats. This creates a loop of hypervigilance, shaping the way that you respond to situations emotionally, physically, and even spiritually.

Feeling Unsafe

One of the hardest parts of living with chronic stress or trauma-like symptoms is the disconnect between your reality and your internal perception. While you may not be in any actual danger, your mind and body perceive your circumstances as potentially harmful.

This disparity is often what puzzles the people in your life and can make your reactions to normal stressors seem like an overreach. On the outside, things might appear stable. You have a job, a home, and supportive people in your life. You may even have a faith that you hold dear. Yet, inside your body, hidden behind that confident smile, your body feels unsettled, guarded, and tense, as if danger is imminent.

This internal (and what seems like eternal) sense of unsafety can be confusing and even discouraging. But it’s important to realize that while your brain may be capable of logical thought, your nervous system isn’t.

Your nervous system doesn’t measure safety through a logical method but relies on experience to gauge danger. If your body has learned that pressure, responsibility, or unpredictability are constant, it may struggle to relax even when the present moment poses no threat.

Responding, Not Reacting

When your nervous system is stuck in survival mode, reactions tend to come faster than reason. You might find yourself snapping at people, emotionally shutting down, overthinking, or withdrawing before you even realize what’s happening. These reactions are protective and are your body’s attempt to keep you safe based on past patterns, not necessarily present-day reality.

To fully overcome your trauma symptoms, you must move away from reaction and into thoughtful and deliberate positive responses. One healthy response comes through self-awareness. Instead of judging yourself harshly for your reactionary tendencies, reframe your response to ask yourself what it is that your body is trying to protect itself from. What is the perceived danger?

While it might seem obvious to you when you slow down your body and mind, the perceived threat might not always be at the forefront of your mind while you’re experiencing your trauma responses. Over time, you’ll begin to see exactly what you’re fearing or feeling threatened by. And when you understand what the threat is, you can work toward neutralizing the threat and overcoming your fear.

This mental reframing will also shift you from self-criticism to curiosity. You can shift ideas like I’m so out of control or “I am always so nervous because I’m always in danger to mere curiosity.” Instead, you could reframe it to “Why am I always nervous when there’s no immediate threat?”

God of Peace

Isn’t it wonderful to know that the God of all Creation, the Prince of Peace Himself, is an active, loving Father who wants to interact with you? It’s comforting to remember that God sees every moment in your life, even the ones where you’re weary and struggling with hidden pain, even when others overlook the pressure you feel because it’s not like traditional trauma.

When you pause and reframe before you react, you open a place where God can meet you. Matthew 11:28-30 extends a beautiful invitation to us. It tells us to come to Jesus when we are burdened. To come to Him when we are weary. And He will give us rest. What an awesome gift rest is to those who have hypervigilance or chronic stress.

When you’re burdened, turn to Him. A quick prayer or a spontaneous song of worship can make a big difference in how you feel. Not only are you inviting the creator of peace into your stress, but you are unloading your burden straight onto His loving and broad shoulders.

Therapy can help

Many people who feel chronic stress but who haven’t had an obvious trauma shy away from therapy. They hesitate to seek help because they believe their stress doesn’t qualify them for professional therapy. They believe that because their trauma experience isn’t clearly defined, they aren’t actually victims of its snares.

But therapy isn’t reserved for worst-case scenarios. It’s a private, safe space where you can start to understand why your body and mind are responding to everyday life in the way they are. You can explore how to interrupt the default emotion of stress in non-threatening situations.

Understanding your chronic stress is the first step toward healing. Your hypervigilance is a signal of perceived danger. It acts as a sign that it’s time to slow down and listen to what your nervous system has been trying to tell you.

If you’re living in survival mode and have been for a long time, learning how to rest can feel uncomfortable and unfamiliar at first. Feeling safe can be relearned. As your body and mind learn how to respond to triggers and stress predictably and healthily, you will start to respond neutrally to things and situations that trigger you now.

This is your invitation and permission to pay attention to your mind and body. Take one intentional step toward stripping away the unexplained trauma in your life. Call our offices to set an appointment with a counselor. A therapist can help you understand your trauma and responses and give you tools that can help you live a fuller, more peaceful life.

item.title: New Women’s Insecurities Brought About by the Digital Era
item.description:
As long as we can remember, women have had to face insurmountable hurdles and overcome great impediments that have contributed to women’s insecurities for centuries.

Women across the world have had to fight for basic human rights such as voting, owning property, and walking without an escort. Sadly, some of our fellow women are still fighting for these rights in other parts of the world to this day.

However, the 21st century has generally brought about a significant reduction in some of these practices against women. Many traditional practices and beliefs that traditionally contributed to women’s insecurities, like gender bias, workplace inequalities, gender-based violence, and social stigmas, were issues modern women thought were behind us.

But just when women had begun to walk in light of this progress, a new and unexpected challenge has emerged, reviving women’s struggles with insecurities yet again.

The Rise of the Digital Era

The digital era, also known as the Digital Revolution or Information Age, began in the mid-twentieth century. It has been marked by the transition from traditional industries to an economy centered on information technology. This has had a profound impact on women, bringing both opportunities and challenges.

Opportunities the digital world has opened for women include:

Economic Empowerment Digital technologies have opened new job opportunities, particularly in tech and remote work, allowing women to balance work and family responsibilities more effectively.

Education and Skills Development Online learning platforms have made education more accessible, enabling women to acquire new skills and advance their careers.

Entrepreneurship The internet has provided a platform for women entrepreneurs to start and grow businesses, reaching global markets with minimal investment.

Advocacy and Activism Social media and digital tools have empowered women to advocate for their rights, raise awareness about gender issues, and mobilize support for social causes.

While the opportunities are immense, the tech era has also introduced new insecurities for women, impacting various aspects of their lives. From biased algorithms to enhanced cybersecurity threats and everything in between, this whole new era is piling on a new set of pressure for women than ever before.

Unexpected Tech-Related Concerns that are Increasing Women’s Insecurities

AI and Algorithm Biases There is already evidence that many of the AI technologies and algorithms being developed can perpetuate gender bias and negative stereotyping. When this technology is applied to hiring processes, women have unfortunately fallen short.

Some studies have shown that job hiring algorithms favor men for technical roles while steering women toward positions requiring skills that are typically lower paid. These job imbalances can make women undervalued or unfairly judged based on biased data.

The Imposter Phenomenon A feeling of not belonging is a common experience for women when it comes to the tech industry. It has been exacerbated by the industry’s gender imbalance, the fast-paced nature of the tech industry, and the high visibility of male tech achievements while female achievements are suppressed.

For example, the gross underrepresentation in tech leadership roles has left many feeling like they aren’t as adequate or competent as their peers in tech.

Rise of Cybersecurity Threats Statistically, women have been targeted more aggressively in cyberattacks such as deepfakes, doxxing, and online harassment. Women who experience online humiliation and cyberbullying can have a pervasive sense of insecurity and fear about their online presence and suffer significant emotional distress, anxiety, and even PTSD.

How Tech-Related Insecurities in Women Manifest

  • Body Image Issues
  • Increased Privacy Concerns
  • Social Isolation
  • Overcompensation
  • Self-Doubt
  • Reluctance to Speak Up

The prevalence of social media platforms has amplified unrealistic beauty standards. Women often feel pressured to conform to these ideals, leading to issues like body dysmorphia, low self-esteem, vulnerability, and fear. To counteract their insecurities, some women may overcompensate by working excessively hard, striving for perfection, or taking on more responsibilities than necessary.

Women in tech may also frequently question their skills and knowledge, feeling as if they aren’t as competent as their male counterparts. This often leads to reluctance to take on challenging projects or apply for leadership roles.

The digital age has blurred the lines between work and personal life, making it challenging for women to maintain a healthy work-life balance, resulting in increased stress and burnout.

All these new women’s insecurities in the digital world highlight the need for greater understanding, dialogue, and resources to help women navigate the digital landscape confidently and safely. There is a need for more inclusive practices and support systems in the tech industry to help women feel secure and valued.

Possible Strategies for Women to Overcome Tech-Based Insecurities

Maintaining work-life balance in the digital age can be challenging, but there are several effective strategies to help manage. Setting clear boundaries, like specific work hours, ensures that everyone in your life knows and respects your personal time.

Other ways to help navigate the complexities of the digital age while maintaining a healthy work-life balance include:

  • Prioritizing ourselves and making time for activities that promote our well-being, such as exercise, cherished hobbies, and relaxation. Regular breaks and physical activity can help mitigate the effects of digital overload.
  • Negotiating flexible work arrangements that suit us as women and mothers and can allow a balance between work and personal commitments. Demanding validation of our unique needs as women, such as flexible hours or remote work options, is not a sign of weakness but rather empowerment.
  • Learning how to use technology mindfully by leveraging productivity tools to manage our time effectively and eliminate the potential for digital distractions. A good tip is to set specific times to check messages, emails, and social pages to avoid constant interruptions.
  • Scheduling regular times for digital detox is crucial to help us as women unwind and unplug from social and work-related technology. This can help to recharge and maintain a healthy balance between being always on and having personal peace of mind.
  • Being realistic and practical about what we can achieve in a day and avoiding overcommitting does not make us less of a woman but rather promotes our wholeness. We don’t have to be “Wonder Woman,” and it’s okay to say no when necessary to prevent burnout and to accept that we don’t have to do extra to prove our worth.

Understanding and addressing these new digital-related issues that are increasing women’s insecurities requires a multifaceted approach, including promoting digital literacy, creating supportive online communities, and advocating for more inclusive practices in tech industries.

As a woman in this fast-paced digital landscape, it’s okay to admit that you need to seek support to get over any hurts and insecurities that you feel. Overcoming tech-related insecurities can be challenging, but professional help can make a significant difference.

Here are some options to consider:

  • A career coach who specializes in tech can provide guidance on career development, skill enhancement, and overcoming workplace challenges.
  • A mentor you can find in your field can provide invaluable support and advice. Mentors share their experiences, offer guidance, and can help you navigate the complexities of the tech industry.
  • An occasional professional development workshop or training session, focused on building technical skills and soft skills, can boost your confidence. Such programs often include networking opportunities, which can also help reduce feelings of isolation.
  • A support group for women in tech can provide a sense of community and shared understanding. Support groups offer emotional support, practical advice, and a platform to share experiences.
  • An online program to bolster your skills on various tech topics is a great morale booster. Enhancing your skills through these courses can help you feel more competent and confident in your abilities.
  • A mindfulness activity like meditation, yoga, or stress management techniques can help you manage anxiety and build resilience.
  • A therapist or counselor can help you explore the root causes of your insecurities, develop strategies to build confidence, and address negative thought patterns.

Women’s insecurities about tech-related matters are more common than any of us may believe, but nothing to be ashamed of.

If you have more questions or would like to talk to a professional about which of these options is best suited for you, you can find specific resources or professionals right here on this website. Call the numbers you see here today.

item.title: Habits That Make Loneliness and Depression Worse
item.description:
It’s perfectly normal to sometimes feel alone, vulnerable, and in need of connection, support, and validation. Many people go through seasons of feeling this way until their situation changes, and they find the help they need. However, others seem to live their lives in a constant state of loneliness and depression, forever frustrated that they can’t seem to connect with anybody, and clueless as to how to change.

Loneliness is not about being alone as much as it’s about feeling unseen and as if you don’t matter. This might have started in childhood, when your needs and wants were dismissed or overlooked by someone who should have been nurturing and loving you. It might be the result of recent trauma that has left you feeling as if you no longer know how to participate in society.

Regardless of the root cause, you have likely picked up habits over the years that have contributed to your feelings of loneliness and depression. You are not forever stuck in this situation, but there is work to do if you are going to get out of it.

When Loneliness and Depression Leave You Feeling Invisible

If you are dealing with loneliness and depression, you might feel as if you are a ghost. It is as if people see through you and as if you make no real impression on anyone around you. This is an awful feeling that you can never get used to, no matter how many years you have experienced it, and you should never have to. People are made for connection, friendships, relationships, and interdependence.

Life is supposed to be complicated and sometimes messy, busy, challenging, and comforting. We are meant to have our hearts broken and then mended, to have love and to give it, to provide support to others, and to receive when we are broken. If you are missing out on these things, you are not to blame.

There could be any number of reasons as to why you are struggling. However, nothing changes until you make it change. It always pays to examine your life and consider what you can do differently.

Habits That Make Loneliness and Depression Worse

People who deal with loneliness and depression are usually stuck in freeze mode. You might have tried to fix your situation, to make friends, and to build relationships, only to fail and feel worse about yourself. Now you are stuck coping with your feelings and doing everything you can to numb your emotions.

So many common, seemingly harmless habits make loneliness and depression harder to deal with. Things like doomscrolling endlessly on your devices, binge-watching shows late into the night and on weekends, and overworking are all valid ways to unwind. However, at some point, these habits are simply keeping you from making changes in your life and are not helping with your underlying issues.

You might be able to stave off feelings of hopelessness and loneliness for the night, but ultimately, you will have to make some changes if you are going to have a breakthrough. Consider the following habits that you might be engaging in, and how you can begin to make changes.

Repressing Your True Feelings

At the root of loneliness and depression for many people is the feeling that no one truly cares. There is a cycle to loneliness and depression that looks a little something like this: you feel as if no one sees you or cares about you, so you isolate and withdraw from all social interactions. Since you have withdrawn from people, they don’t see you, and it logically follows that you feel unseen.

When you are in a social situation, even in a workspace, you remain closed off and silent. The people around you either assume that you are uninterested in connection, even polite interest, or that you are quiet because you are content.

Lonely people dealing with depression don’t often appear to be lonely or depressed. They paste smiles on their faces, pretend to be confident, and convince themselves that they are fine. This is a form of emotional dishonesty, and it is the exact opposite of intimacy and connection.

It’s risky to let people into your life and to share your struggles. There are instances and occasions where it would be inappropriate to wear your heart on your sleeve, such as in a professional environment. It isn’t helpful to withdraw all the time. You will never connect with someone meaningfully until you can be vulnerable and honest about your emotions and battles.

Downplaying Your Needs

Have you ever found yourself agreeing to do something you would rather not do, only to feel resentful and bitter about it afterward? Perhaps you feel as if you can’t let others down, despite constantly being let down and disappointed yourself. People who deal with loneliness and depression will often downplay their preferences, needs, and wants.

When you have a decade or more of unmet needs, you will naturally feel as if you are not worth anyone’s time or effort, or as if your needs and preferences matter less than others. In the end, you will feel less worthy of love and attention, and isolated with a host of genuine needs that have gone unmet.

It takes time and practice to find your voice and speak up for yourself, but you can start by asking yourself what you need, what you want, and what you prefer. This can apply to any situation.

For example, you might like to have a quiet morning at work with minimal small talk. You have every right to inform your colleagues that you are focusing on your tasks, but that you would love to hear their stories later during your lunch break. Each time you value your needs, preferences, and wants, you are giving something deeply important to yourself, kind of like watering a dry and thirsty plant.

Bristling

Although you don’t want to face most of your feelings, there is one feeling that will constantly surface, and that is anger. Anger is not always a bad emotion to feel; in fact, most people feel angry when they experience something unfair or unjust. When you are overlooked, unseen, and unheard by those around you, it is understandable and even logical to be angry.

While you may not express your emotions, others often feel your anger in interactions with you. You may appear irritable, short-tempered, sharp, or cold. It is not your intention to communicate these things, but many people will keep their distance from you because of your bristling demeanor.

Most people who deal with loneliness and depression have been policing their tone and adjusting their body language for a long time. It is exhausting and ineffective as far as making connections goes.

The only way to become emotionally honest with yourself and others is to face your emotional needs. The problem is not the anger you feel or the prickly way you communicate with those around you. That is a symptom of deeper emotional needs that have gone unmet for too long.

A Better Solution for Loneliness and Depression

The reason these habits don’t help in the long run is that they are not about changing your situation; they are about coping with your feelings. In the end, your feelings are numbed and suppressed, and you are stuck in the same situation that caused your loneliness and depression in the first place.

Loneliness and depression are soul-crushing things to deal with. However, you are not a victim, and you don’t have to remain in your current situation. Regardless of how things feel now, there is a brighter future ahead of you if you will only begin to help yourself.

One of the best things you can do if you are dealing with loneliness and depression is to get counseling. It would be my honor and deepest goal to provide a safe space for you to express yourself and journey with you for as long as you need support. Please consult with my reception team if you would like to investigate further.

I’m cheering you on!
